segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul and Timothy, slaves of Christ Jesus, to all the holy ones in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I thank my God every time I remember you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: always, in every prayer of mine for all of you, making my prayer with joy,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because of your partnership in the good news from the first day until now.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am confident of this very thing: that the one who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is right for me to think this way about all of you, because I hold you in my heart, for you are all partners with me in grace, both in my chains and in the defence and confirmation of the good news.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God is my witness how I long for all of you with the deep affection of Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this is what I pray: that your love may overflow still more and more in knowledge and all insight,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you may discern what really matters, and so be sincere and blameless for the day of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that what has happened to me has actually turned out for the progress of the good news,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that it has become clear throughout the whole imperial guard and to everyone else that my chains are in Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and most of the brothers and sisters, having gained confidence in the Lord from my chains, dare all the more to speak the word without fear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some, it is true, proclaim Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The latter act out of love, knowing that I am placed here for the defence of the good news;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the former announce Christ out of selfish ambition, not from pure motives, thinking to stir up distress for me in my chains.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What does it matter? Only that in every way, whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is announced, and in this I rejoice. Yes, and I will go on rejoicing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for I know that this will turn out for my deliverance through your prayers and the support of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in keeping with my eager expectation and hope that I will not be put to shame in anything, but that with all boldness, now as always, Christ will be honoured in my body, whether through life or through death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if I am to live on in the flesh, that means fruitful work for me—and which I will choose I cannot say.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am hard pressed between the two: I have the desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And confident of this, I know that I will remain, and remain with all of you, for your progress and joy in the faith,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that your boasting in Christ Jesus may overflow on my account, through my presence with you again.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Only live as citizens in a way worthy of the good news of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear about you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one soul striving side by side for the faith of the good news,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and in no way frightened by those who oppose you. To them this is a sign of destruction, but of your salvation, and that from God;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for to you it has been granted, on behalf of Christ, not only to believe in him but also to suffer on his behalf,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as you face the same struggle you saw in me and now hear of in me.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and “servant” softens it. In the Septuagint “slave of the Lord” is also a title of honour for figures such as Moses and David, so the word carries both lowliness and dignity. Many translations keep “servants”; others use “slaves” or “bondservants”.

“Saints” now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word of every member of the community, as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God's people” or “his holy people”.

The first term was an everyday word for a supervisor or official. It later developed into “bishop”, but here it is plural within a single city and refers to a group of local leaders. The second term, elsewhere simply “servant”, here names a recognised role in the assembly. The exact duties of either group at this date are not known.

“Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for the public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel”.

notes.traditional: it is right / it is meet
notes.note: The adjective is the one this translation normally renders “righteous” or “just”. In the impersonal idiom used here it means simply “right” or “fitting”, and “righteous” would not be English. It belongs to the same word family as “righteousness” in verse 11; Greek has one family where English divides it between right/righteous and just/justice.

notes.phrase: I hold you in my heart
notes.traditional: I have you in my heart
notes.note: The Greek can equally be read “because you hold me in your heart”, since either pronoun can be the subject. The word order slightly favours “I hold you”, and most translations take it that way, but a few adopt the other reading.

The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as family, and this letter is plainly written to the whole community, women included (see 4:2–3). “Brothers” alone now sounds exclusively male. Several modern translations render it the same way; others keep “brothers”.

The Greek borrows the Latin praetorium, which could mean a governor's official residence in a province or the emperor's praetorian guard in Rome. “Everyone else” suggests a body of people, which is why the guard is chosen here. Which is meant depends on where Paul was imprisoned. Rome is the traditional answer, but Ephesus and Caesarea have also been proposed, and the question is not settled.

Many early manuscripts read “the word of God” and a few “the word of the Lord”. The SBLGNT prints the shorter reading, taking the longer forms to be scribal clarifications. The sense is the same either way.

This is the word rendered “salvation” in verse 28. Here it may mean release from prison, or Paul's final vindication before God whether he lives or dies; the next verse (“whether through life or through death”) leads many scholars to prefer the second. The clause echoes the Greek version of Job 13:16, where Job expects to be vindicated.

The word covers both arriving and being present. It is the term used elsewhere for the coming of Christ and, in ordinary Greek, for the visit of a ruler. Here it refers simply to Paul's being with the Philippians again.

notes.traditional: let your manner of life be / conduct yourselves
notes.note: The verb means to live as a citizen and fulfil one's civic duties, though it could be used more loosely for conduct in general. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens prized their status, and Paul returns to the image in 3:20. Most translations render it generally as “conduct yourselves”; a number of scholars and some versions bring out the civic sense, as here.

candidates.reason: Translators split between “servant”, “slave” and “bondservant”, and the register already presupposes “slave” in its διάκονος entry without listing δοῦλος itself.
The plural address recurs in every letter and Acts, and readers would be misled if it were “brothers” in some chapters and “brothers and sisters” in others.
It ranges from neutral bodily life (as here) to Paul's morally charged sense, and translations vary between “flesh”, “body”, “sinful nature” and “human nature”.
It is rendered “soul”, “life”, “self” or “mind” across the New Testament, and “soul” often imports a later body–soul dualism.
The word covers rescue from danger and final salvation, and a rule is needed for when “deliverance” replaces “salvation”.

patch.reason: euangelion promoted to active after full-run drift (good news 37 / gospel 35)
